title: Cocoa vs. coffee: caffeine and other differences

seo.title: Cocoa vs. coffee: caffeine and differences
seo.meta_description: Which has more caffeine, cocoa or coffee? Compare normal drink servings—not 100 g of powder—and understand cocoa's much higher theobromine content.
seo.search_intent: Compare caffeine and key differences between cocoa and coffee

excerpt: A normal cup of coffee generally provides several times more caffeine than a cocoa drink. EFSA estimates about 90 mg in 200 mL filter coffee; 5–10 g of the USDA natural cocoa reference would provide roughly 12–23 mg. Cocoa instead contains much more theobromine.
content_html:
Comparing 100 g of dry coffee with 100 g of cocoa is nutritionally neat and practically useless. You do not make both drinks with the same amount of dry material. The fair question is how much caffeine ends up in a normal cup.

Normal servings put coffee clearly ahead

EFSA uses approximate guide values of 90 mg caffeine for 200 mL filter coffee and 80 mg for a 60 mL espresso. The USDA natural unsweetened cocoa reference contains 230 mg caffeine per 100 g.

That makes 5 g cocoa about 12 mg caffeine and 10 g about 23 mg. On that basis, the filter coffee contains roughly four to eight times as much caffeine.

Drink or ingredientApprox. caffeine
Filter coffee, 200 mL90 mg
Espresso, 60 mL80 mg
Natural cocoa, 5 g~12 mg
Natural cocoa, 10 g~23 mg

Both foods vary. Brew strength, bean species, grind, and extraction change coffee; cultivar and cocoa processing change cocoa.

Cocoa's main methylxanthine is not caffeine

Cocoa contains much more theobromine. The USDA entry lists about 2,057 mg/100 g theobromine versus 230 mg caffeine. A 5.4 g tablespoon works out to roughly 111 mg theobromine.

That helps explain why cocoa and coffee are not physiologically identical, but 111 mg theobromine is not equivalent to 111 mg caffeine. They are related compounds with different effects.

The drinks are nutritionally different too

Black brewed coffee is mostly water and extracted compounds, so it contributes very few calories on its own. Cocoa powder is a solid food containing fiber, protein, fat, carbohydrate, and minerals. A tablespoon of unsweetened cocoa contributes around 12 calories before milk or sugar.

A finished cocoa drink can therefore be much more calorie-dense than black coffee while still containing less caffeine.

Which is better if you want less caffeine?

A modest cocoa drink generally wins on caffeine quantity, but it is not zero-caffeine. Very sensitive people may still notice it. Total daily intake from tea, soda, chocolate, energy drinks, and other sources matters too.

There is no fixed conversion

It is tempting to say one mug of cocoa equals one-quarter of a coffee, but products vary too widely. A strongly brewed coffee can exceed the guide value, while an alkalized cocoa can contain much less caffeine than the natural reference.

The robust conclusion is narrower: coffee is usually the much larger caffeine source per drink; cocoa provides less caffeine, much more theobromine, and an entirely different food matrix.

faq.question: Which has more caffeine, cocoa or coffee?
faq.answer: Coffee in a normal serving. EFSA lists about 90 mg in 200 mL filter coffee, while 5–10 g of the USDA natural cocoa reference provides roughly 12–23 mg.

faq.question: Can cocoa replace coffee if I want less caffeine?
faq.answer: It can substantially reduce caffeine when used in modest amounts, but cocoa still contains caffeine and theobromine.

faq.question: Is theobromine the same as caffeine?
faq.answer: No. Both are methylxanthines, but their potency and effects differ, so milligrams are not directly interchangeable.

faq.question: Does black coffee have fewer calories than cocoa?
faq.answer: Usually yes. Plain brewed coffee contributes very little energy; cocoa powder contains fat, protein, carbohydrate, and fiber. Milk and sweeteners can change either drink.
